label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
Nana,

Denise is going to read you this in the kitchen, so I'm picturing you at the table with a cup of tea going cold, and I hope you can hear me being a little bit of a mess. I've started this letter about six times and closed the laptop each time, so I'm going to stop trying to get it perfect and just write it.

First: I'm proud of you. You picked Elmwood yourself. Nobody made you. Plenty of people your age get moved somewhere by their kids because the kids are worried, and then they spend the next two years being grumpy about it. You looked at the options, you went and saw the place, you decided, and you're the one who got it done. Fifty-one years on Kathleen Street, and you didn't wait for something to force your hand. That's you. That's exactly you.

I know you're going to tell me not to feel guilty about not being there. Everyone's already told me it's fine, and I know it is. I'm on call that whole week, and I couldn't find anyone to trade with, and it's a bad week to be the one with the pager. But I'd be lying if I said I wasn't sad about missing it. So I'm going to sit here and be sad about it for one paragraph, and then I'll stop.

Here's what I keep coming back to. That house is yours. Grandpa Walt was the one who built the shed and fixed the gutters, but you're the one who raised half the family in that kitchen. Every birthday, every argument, every bowl of soup someone needed after a bad day, happened at that table, and you were always the one at the stove. I don't think anyone ever told you that properly, so I'm telling you now: the house was you. Denise is taking the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest, which is fair, because she's the one who'll actually wind the clock. I asked for the crib board, and I know you'll think that's the only thing I cared about. It's not. It's just the thing I can carry with me.

Some of my favourite memories are from summers at the house. You let me stay up to watch the Expos on that little TV on the counter, as long as I dried the dishes first. I'm pretty sure I dried every dish you owned by the end of the summer, and some of them twice, because I was so slow about it. You never once told me to hurry up. You'd just keep washing until I'd finished, and then you'd say "Go on, the game's on," like you hadn't been waiting for me the whole time.

And the back steps. I don't think you know how much I loved those mornings. You'd be out there at six with your tea, and I'd come out in my socks, and you wouldn't say a word until the cup was empty. At first I thought you were just grumpy in the morning. Then I figured out it was the best part of your day and you didn't want anybody talking into it. I still do that sometimes, sit with my coffee and don't say anything for a while. I learned it from you.

Now, the crib. You taught me when I was about seven, and you never once let me win. Not once. I'd cry, you'd say "Count your hand, sweetheart," and you'd peg out before I'd even finished adding. When I finally skunked you at fifteen, I was so proud I could hardly stand it, and you made me a whole pan of butter tarts. I think about that a lot. You didn't make it easy for me, and then when I earned it, you made sure I knew it was a big deal. That's pretty much the whole way you love people.

When I got the job in Toronto, you mailed me a twenty-dollar bill taped inside a card that said "for pizza, you look thin on the computer." I still have the card. I've never spent the twenty. I'm not sure I ever will.

I'm also going to put it on record that last Christmas, my pager went off in the middle of dinner, and you looked over at me and asked, very seriously, whether the internet was broken again, and whether I'd fixed it. Everyone at the table laughed. Then ever since, every time I call, your first question is "Did anything break?" I've come to think that's your way of checking that I'm okay, which is very sweet and also a little bit insulting, because nothing's broken. Mostly. I'm going to keep telling you the truth, though. If something's ever broken, I'll let you know.

I'm told Elmwood has a crib league. I'm told you're going to clean them out, and I want you to go easy on them, because at least two of those women are going to be cheating, and I'd like you to be the first person to notice and say so. You've spent your whole life teaching people how to count their hands honestly. You can do the same thing for a bunch of church ladies on Tuesdays. I'm also told your room looks out at the parking lot and a big maple. I hope the maple is spectacular in the fall, and I hope you get to watch it change colour through the window with a cup of tea, because you deserve a view that does a bit of the work for you.

I hope the move goes smoothly. I hope the movers are gentle with the china and the clock, and that Denise doesn't let you carry anything heavy. And I hope that when you get to Elmwood and the first night is long and quiet, you know that you're still exactly who you were in that kitchen. Different address, same woman who never let anybody win, and who somehow still managed to make everyone feel loved.

Thank you for the crib games, the butter tarts, the dishes, the back steps, the twenty dollars, and the hundreds of times you made a kitchen feel like home. I love you more than I can get into a letter.

I'll be up on December 5th, once rotation's over. I'll bring the good cards. You bring the board, or just tell me where it is, and we'll sit down at the new place and have our first game. I'm going to lose. I'm going to lose badly. And I'm going to ask you to count my hand for me, one more time.

Love you, Nana.

See you on the 5th.

Your grandson,
[Your name]
